texts.body:
Promo (part 1)
Welcome to LOGUS for beginners
the first part of the bestselling English course on Udemy
LOGUS is a very intensive spoken English course
in the form of a cartoon
designed for people who are tired
of learning the language from those boring textbooks
and listening to nerdy teachers
It was created for people
who want to finally learn to think in English
and to speak it fluently
just like their native language
You think it’s impossible?
We’ll prove you wrong.
This course begins with the most basic things
you need to start speaking
and it gradually goes into the intermediate level
towards the end of the course
And the best part is
you start speaking instantly
Right from the first lesson
Isn’t that cool?
And make no mistake here
this is not your supplementary short course
this is a full-blown course
that guides you from the very basics of the English language
to the Intermediate level step by step.
100% of the lesson is speaking
in a form of a dialogue
You listen
answer and ask questions
and immediately see if you’ve made a mistake
And if you did
nothing to worry about
because you will repeat every grammar construction
so many times later on
that they will all be recorded directly in your brain
without drowning you in the grammar rules.
Where it’s necessary
you’ll be given very clear and simple explanations
of essential grammar
And at the end of each chapter
you will take a milestone test
to check your progress.
You will learn over 1000 of the most important English words
and phrases
And by learning
I don’t mean memorizing
I mean learning in such a way
that you can use them effortlessly in your speech without thinking
Each lesson you’ll be hearing and saying over 1200 words
That amount of language practice is enough
to make you a fluent speaker in no time
And just imagine how many more job opportunities you will have
with fluent English like this
And this course is a must-have component for you
if you’re planning to take IELTS or TOEFL tests in the future.
So, if you want to stop speaking English like a potato
when traveling
studying
or when talking to your business partners
this is the right course for you
Buy it now for this special promo price
before it goes ALL the way up!
And with the 30-day return policy,
this is a safe bet.
Click that buy button right now
and learn to speak English
once and for all
texts.title: Promo (part 1)

texts.body:
Instruction (part 2)
Welcome to the tutorial video
Watch it till the very end
in order to avoid confusion about what you should do
and how this course works.
What exactly is going to happen starting from the next video?
You’ll learn the new vocabulary and grammar,
then I’ll be asking you lots and lots of questions
on different topics
When you see this message
it means you have to start answering the question aloud
Not in whisper
not to yourself
You have to speak aloud
Moreover
you have to pronounce the full answer to the question
For example,
if I ask you
Where do you live?
you’ll have to answer
I live in my apartment
The answer like
uh… in my apartment
is not going to cut it
Always give the full answer
I’ll give you just enough time to answer the question
After that
you’ll hear the correct answer
If your answer is different in grammar
or in vocabulary
stop the video
try to analyze your mistake
go back a few seconds
and repeat the right answer after me
If the time I give you to answer isn’t enough
it means you have to speed up the pace
Go through the same lesson one more time
until you can fit in the timeframe
If you stop the video to give yourself more time to answer
, it’s cheating
Don’t do that
When you see this message
you have to repeat the question I asked you
So, pay close attention to the questions I ask
Translations
You will hear all the dialogues
new vocabulary and grammar in English
But I bet you’ll want to have it all translated
If you’re using a computer
click on the “CC” button below
If you’re using a mobile app
tap on the video while playing it
and at the top
you will see the “CC” menu
tap on it
and choose the language
you want vocabulary and grammar
to be translated into
But regardless of the language you choose
all the dialogues will appear in English only
Vocabulary and grammar parts will be translated
Repetition
If you want to learn to think in English
repetition is extremely important
That’s why each lesson begins with repetition
of what you learned before
Do not skip the repetition
and go straight to the new material
This way you will never become fluent
1 lesson at a time
The lessons are pretty long
So, make sure you have about an hour and a half
for your English each day
without being disturbed
For the maximum effect
you should take one lesson each day
But make sure you take not less than 3 lessons per week
Good luck
And see you in the lesson 1

If you want to understand English grammar and English spelling

What is “a” and when do we use it?
“A” is an article
We use it before singular nouns
It might sound weird to you
especially if you don’t have articles in your native language
But they are very important in English
So, always put the article “a”

one of many

Now let’s see what happens in simple present tense
when the subject is “he”, “she” or "it"
We just add the ending “s”
or “es”
to the verb
For example
I drink 2 cups of coffee in the morning
but
he drinks 2 cups of coffee in the morning
You see the ending “s” here?
Good
We put it here
because the subject is “he”
Jenifer likes her car
“Likes”
with the ending “s”
because the subject is “Jenifer”
it’s a she
There are a couple of exceptions here
The verb “have”
We don’t just add “s” to it
There is no such word “haves”
When the subject is “he”, “she” or "it"
“have”
turns into
“has”
French fries have a lot of salt in them
But
this cake has a lot of sugar in it
This cake is “it”
“It has”
"this cake has"
In questions
our indicative word
the one we put before the subject
is not “do”
but
“does”.
or example:
Does John drive a car?
Subject “John”,
it’s a “he”,
ore it we have the indicative word “does”
and after it we have our verb “drive”
Notice that it doesn’t have the ending “s” anymore
Another example
How many cups of coffee does Lisa drink in the morning?
The same story
Subject "Lisa"
before it we have the indicative word “does”
because Lisa is a she
and after it
we have our verb “drink”
without the ending “s”
In negative
we put “does not”
or its contraction
“doesn’t”
after the subject
For example
John doesn’t have a car
Lisa doesn’t like tea
Sarah doesn’t work hard
"Who" in questions
Let’s look at this example
John likes Lisa
And now let’s ask questions with “Who”
2 questions, actually
In one
“who” will be about John
and in another one,
about “Lisa”.
So, if we know that John likes somebody
but we don’t know who he likes
we ask in the following way:
Who does John like?
Subject “John”,
before it
we have our indicative word “does”
and after it
we have our main verb “like”
Who does John like?
And what if we know that somebody likes Lisa
but we don’t know who
and we want to ask a question about it
we do it this way
who likes Lisa?
something’s strange here
We don’t have an indicative word “does”
Why not?
Well, let’s look closer.
We have our main verb here, “likes”
but do we have the subject?
No, we don’t.
It’s unknown
So, if we don’t have the subject,
we don’t put an indicative word before it.
Let’s see another example
Mason lives with his parents
And now let’s ask two questions with “who”
in one
his parents will be unknown
in the second one
Mason will be unknown
Who does Mason live with?
We have our subject Mason
before it we have our indicative word “does”
and after it
e have our main verb “live”
without the ending “s”
Who lives with his parents?
Here the subject is unknown
Mason is unknown
Instead of Mason
we have “who”
No subject
no indicative word “does”
You’ll understand it better in practice

We use the word “some”
with unspecified
very general objects or people
or with the unspecified
quantity or number of objects or people
For example

I didn’t count how much water exactly is on the floor

We use “some”
in positive statements and in questions
For example
Do you have some money?
Do you want some coffee?
There is another word with a similar meaning
“any”
but we use it in questions and negative statements
For example
Do you have any money?
Positive answer:
Yes, I have some money
negative answer:
No, I don’t have any money.
Do you know any people at Microsoft?
Positive response:
Yes, I know some people at Microsoft.
Negative response:
No, I don’t know any people at Microsoft.
And there is another word
“no”
which is only used in negative sentences
You can say
I don’t drink any coffee in the morning
or
I drink no coffee in the morning
I don’t have any money
or
I have no money
I don’t see any cars in the street
or
I see no cars in the street
Again
we use "some" in positive sentences and in questions
"Any"
in questions and in negative sentences
and “no”
only in negative sentences

There are several verbs in English
that behave in a different way than all other verbs
In order not to make things too complicated for you
let’s just call these words
“special”
One of these special words is “can”
which means “be able to”
Let’s look at several examples
I can speak English
We can drink three bottles of whiskey in a few hours
"what’s so special about this word" you might ask?
keep looking
He can stay under water for 4 minutes
Still not seeing it?
Look here
We didn’t add “s” here
although the subject is “he”
She can cook a chocolate cake for the party
no “s” here either
We don’t say
She CANS cook a chocolate cake for the party
So, the first special thing about “can” is
we don’t add “s” to it
Another thing
questions
If the statement looks like this
He can stay under water for 4 minutes
the question will look like this
DOES he can stay under water for 4 minutes?
No-no-no-no-no!
I’m just kidding.
It’s not how we ask a question with “can”
Look carefully
Can he stay under water for 4 minutes?
“He can stay”
“can he stay?”
How long can he stay under water?
"Can he stay?"
Where can he stay for 4 minutes?
"Can he stay?"
Statement:
She can cook a chocolate cake for the party
Question:
Can she cook a chocolate cake for the party?
"She can"
"can she?"
How many chocolate cakes can she cook for the party?
When can she cook a chocolate cake?
One more special thing about “can”
negative statements
In negative statements,
we use “cannot”
or its contraction
“can’t”
I can’t stay under water for 10 minutes
She can’t cook 10 cakes in one hour
